To us, Jesus is the shepherd whose flock this was before it was ever ours to keep. He is the one who will ask us what became of the people placed in our care. Peter was a good shepherd, Paul was one, and so were the bishops who came after them, and Cyprian. Yet to good shepherds he commended one good Shepherd, and that is who Jesus is to us.

His death and rising are not facts we simply affirm and set aside. His cross, his burial, his rising on the third day, his going up to the Father — these were ordered deliberately. The life we lead here was cut to their shape, not only mystically but in reality. We crucify our own flesh: that is his cross in us. We are buried with him in the water: that is his burial in us. We walk in a life made new: that is his rising in us. We set our affection on what is above, our life hidden with him in God. That is his ascension and his sitting at God's right hand, worked out in an ordinary life.

He is also the one by whose grace any good in us exists at all. Whatever good a person does was given to them before they did it.
